The NewHorizon sample is generally skewed towards being more lopsided than naive expectations. This cautions against using dark matter or under-resolved hydrodynamic simulations as a null-hypothesis to compare to real systems. We find broad, hemispheric lopsidedness to be much more prevalent than narrow lopsidedness inherited from group infall. Across all systems, the dividing plane between the richest and emptiest hemispheres is systematically aligned with a nearby intermediate-scale cosmic filament. Further analysis reveals that the lopsidedness of systems is largely inherited from that of the network of filaments feeding them. The most populated side almost systematically contains the highest number of filaments. Such anisotropies of local filament networks are often indicative of on-going or recent zippers (filament merger $<2$ Gyr). Converging filamentary structures therefore funnel satellites preferentially onto one side of host halos, naturally generating lopsided configurations without requiring galaxy mergers. Twister remnants (of high orbital momentum mergers of filaments) are also found on the richest hemisphere of our systems, perhaps reminiscent of vorticity preventing mergers hence causing satellites' pooling. These results suggest that lopsidedness is primarily an outcome of the evolution of the intermediate-scale cosmic web. This highlights the need for increased hydrodynamic resolution in simulations.

title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
summary:
Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations.
  We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at https://github.com/AMDResearch/kiwi.

title: ReflectScene:MLLM-Guided Closed-Loop Diffusion for 3D Indoor Scene Generation
summary: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence.We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising.Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.

title: Weighing the Envelope: Component Weight and Arbitration in Envelope-Layer Defenses for a Single LLM Agent
summary: The envelope layer is the channel through which malicious content enters an LLM agent. Prior work established label and memory effects on multi-agent A2A envelopes, but the weight structure when MCP tools and memory coexist in a single agent remains unclear. Our threat model assumes an attacker pre-plants a malicious tool and poisons long-term memory; a benign user request inadvertently triggers it, and the attacker never enters the conversation. Following GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D, we measure how labels, memory, tool roles, and the backend shape invocation decisions across label-memory conflict, tool roles, robustness, and tool generalization. A tool-side forced-verification label substantially reduces semantic breach, but strong success memory pulls it back; a memory-side downgrade statement returns the outcome to the level of the label alone. The label works through mandatory implementation inspection plus default denial, not length or format; memory authorization wording erodes it with dose, while position and multi-turn pressure do not change the defense direction. Tool roles divide label effects into substitution, suppression, and boundary failure: low penetration is not safety, local leakage is the main residual risk, and a second malicious tool shows the same direction. Envelope labels are not a switch but a measurable, reversible weight constrained by backend and tool role, acting as a soft gate and risk signal within a broader defense rather than a substitute for permissions, sandboxing, or human review.

title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

title: Re-Testing LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translations Against Their Original C
summary: Most C-to-Rust translators use large language models (LLMs), and each reports a success rate from its own correctness check. We survey 34 C-to-Rust translators that use LLMs. Only one reports testing its check, and eleven release the original C and their Rust in runnable form. We re-test all eleven. We run the C and the Rust on generated inputs, compare every output, and count a divergence only where the C has no undefined behavior. All eleven release defective translations: we find 160 defects, 93 of them outright errors on ordinary inputs. Their own checks accepted 86 defective translations. For 81 of them, the released check never compared the programs on an input that exposes the defect. For three of the other five, it ran one but compared only part of the output. A success rate is only as good as its check. Before counting a translation as a success, authors should compare every output with the C's on inputs the repair loop never saw, check that a verifier reaches its assertion, release exactly what the check accepted, and report how they tested the check.

title: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.

title: Materials representations organize transferable supervision for chemical extrapolation
summary: Materials discovery often requires chemical extrapolation beyond labeled data. When target compounds contain elements absent from training, which compounds of other elements provide transferable supervision remains unclear. Here we show that, without target-property labels, materials representations rank other elements by the supervision their compounds provide. Engineered descriptors rank them largely by elemental-property similarity, whereas a pretrained crystal-graph encoder ranks them by the geometry of its learned representation. At fixed training-set size, excluding the compounds of the encoder's six top-ranked elements raises formation-energy and bandgap errors by 100-110 meV per atom and 42-85 meV, versus little change for six lower-ranked elements. The rankings hold across properties, regressors and datasets. The encoder's ranking outperforms elemental-property similarity and periodic groups, suggesting that it captures how elements behave within compounds. Materials representations thus organize transferable supervision, which can be identified before model training, informing dataset assessment and label acquisition.

title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

title: Unpolarized Generalized Parton Distributions of the Nucleon in a Covariant Quark-Diquark Approach
summary: We study the unpolarized generalized parton distributions (GPDs) of the nucleon in a covariant quark-diquark approach, in which both scalar and axial-vector diquarks are treated as composite subsystems. Motivated by previous form factor studies, we introduce a vertex correction based on the pion cloud picture as a first exploratory treatment of pion cloud effects at the GPD level, in order to improve the description of $E^q(ξ, x, t)$ and related magnetic observables. At the model input scale, only valence quarks are included. With the vertex correction, the electromagnetic form factors $G_{E, M}$ and the mass form factor $A$ obtained from the Mellin moments of the GPDs agree well with those obtained from direct calculations. The vertex correction brings the evolved charge weighted distribution $\sum{e^q E^q(ξ, x, t)}$ closer to the phenomenological parametrization. The correction shifts transverse strength from the central region toward the peripheral region, consistent with the long range character of the pion cloud contribution. The transverse structure results further suggest a harder longitudinal momentum distribution in the central region of the nucleon than in its periphery. Furthermore, the evolved real part of the proton Compton form factor, $\mathrm{Re} \mathcal{H}(ξ, t)$, has a reasonable magnitude and follows the main trend of the Quantum Deep Neural Networks (QDNN) extraction. In addition, $\mathrm{Re} \mathcal{H}$ may be more sensitive to the ERBL region than the other physical quantities calculated in this work.

title: Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games
summary: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.

title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

title: Metrics-in-the-Loop: Complexity Feedback Reshapes Agent-Written Code
summary: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.

title: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards
summary: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

title: Breaking the Myth of Four-Tier Stacked Transistors for Logic: an Investigation from Process to Device and Block-Level PPA
summary: For the first time, this work evaluated whether 4-tier stacked transistors can translate the straightforward density gains into realistic chip-level scaling benefits. A practical dual-sided 4-tier transistor-stacking CFFET (Flipped CFET-to-CFET) process was proposed, on which a DTCO framework spanning standard-cell design, local interconnects, RO analysis, and physical implementation was built under 2A node design rules. The CFFET was also benchmarked with its 2-tier transistor-stacking counterparts FFET. Among CFFET configurations, the best-performing Symmetric Power still lags FFET by 11.2% in RO frequency due to the complex MOL parasitics. At the block level, CFFET reduces the Ibex RISC-V core area by only 12.8% (far below the 40% nominal cell-height reduction), while running 10.9% slower at iso-power. We further introduced a novel Tetris-like cell stitching to minimize the area overhead, which allows non-rectangular cell design and recovers 7.4% area in a 1-bit ALU design. An optimized NanoStack CFFET was finally proposed, inspired by previous work. This work indicates that straightforward vertical 4-tier stacking proves insufficient to guarantee enough PPA benefits, though the resulting design insights may guide future advanced architectures.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of the Toda lattice
summary: In this paper we consider the Toda lattice under random, spatially inhomogeneous initial data, meaning that its initial momenta and interparticle spacings are independent and their laws may slowly vary in space. When the density is strictly positive (but sufficiently small), we identify the model's hydrodynamic limit under Euler scaling. More precisely, we prove that spatial averages of each of the model's local conserved quantities converge to moments of a density $m_τ(λ,q)$ solving the generalized hydrodynamic equation predicted by Doyon arXiv:1902.07624 and Spohn arXiv:1902.07751. To do so, we justify the notion that the Toda lattice can be thought of as a dense collection of many "quasiparticles" that interact through scattering. As in Aggarwal arXiv:2503.08018, we define these quasiparticles through spectral properties of the Toda Lax matrix, but in our inhomogeneous setting we must now show that the eigenvectors of this Lax matrix remain localized throughout the dynamics. The core of our work is to show that, with high probability, the quasiparticle trajectories converge to the characteristic curves of the generalized hydrodynamic equation.

title: Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
summary: This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting. The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used. Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted. The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2). Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) separates long-run trends from monsoon and crop-cycle seasonality. A non-negative PCA gives sign-consistent, interpretable weights and rankings nearly identical to standard PCA ($ρ$ = 0.998). Across districts, the index explains 74% of the variation in the NFHS-5 wealth index, 52% in household consumption (HCES 2023-24) and about 78% in real district GDP levels (65% in logs), but does not track short-run output growth. Because it measures structural capacity rather than annual output, the index kept rising through the FY2020-21 COVID-19 contraction. Across Maharashtra's six revenue divisions, relative inequality fell by 44% even as the absolute gap between leading and lagging divisions widened by 32%; district-level $β$-convergence implies a half-life of about 14 years. The framework offers a scalable, deflator-free basis for structural monitoring in data-sparse economies.

title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
summary: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

title: Mitigating the Grid Impact of Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers via High-Fidelity Model Flexibility
summary: Gigawatt-scale artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are being connected at a single point of interconnection (POI) faster than transmission can be reinforced, yet studies of their flexibility rely on DC power flow and simplified load envelopes that omit voltage, cooling dynamics, and workload deadlines. This paper addresses this gap by embedding a high-fidelity AIDC model, with separate inference and training pools, hall thermal mass, PV, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with reactive capability, and a STATCOM, in a five-minute multi-period AC optimal power flow. Simulations on the RTS-GMLC test system show that active-power flexibility mitigates local price spikes and relieves congestion, whereas reactive support from the BESS inverter or a STATCOM is needed to keep the POI voltage away from sagging around its 0.95~pu limit. Sensitivity analyses show that cost-driven charging of large batteries can induce new morning congestion and that storage largely substitutes for wider workload deferral.

title: DetectViT: Test-time Backdoor Detection for Vision Transformers via Inter-Head Attention Discrepancy
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: $\textit{complete attention hijacking}$, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and $\textit{partial attention hijacking}$, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose $\textbf{DetectViT}$, a test-time backdoor detection method that requires neither training data, model outputs, nor any prior knowledge of the trigger. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64--128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of $100\%$ and a false positive rate of $0.17\%$ on BadCLIP. Notably, it introduces negligible additional overhead by relying solely on attention weights already computed during inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/siquanhuang/DetectViT.

title: Beyond Intelligibility: Fine-Grained Perceptual Assessment of Dysarthric Speech with Auditory Large Language Models
summary: Accurate assessment of dysarthric speech is vital for clinical diagnosis and rehabilitation, yet existing automated methods rely heavily on isolated, single-task models or generic speech quality metrics that fail to disentangle heterogeneous neuromotor deficits. This work presents the first systematic investigation into adapting auditory large language models (ALLMs) for multi-dimensional dysarthric speech assessment under a unified, prompt-conditioned framework. Four representative ALLMs are benchmarked across five clinical perceptual dimensions from the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP): naturalness, monopitch, intelligibility, imprecise consonants, and inappropriate silences. To bridge generic perceptual quality and clinical evaluation, a two-stage training paradigm is explored, leveraging out-of-domain pre-training followed by in-domain clinical adaptation. Experimental results demonstrate that leading ALLMs reliably capture fine-grained pathological variations, exhibiting distinct and complementary strengths across prosodic and articulatory attributes. These findings establish ALLMs as a scalable foundation for clinical speech evaluation and provide practical insights into model selection and multi-task transfer potential.

title: Mean Curvature Minimizing Foliations Of A Vector Field
summary: Streamline patterns are ubiquitous in nature. Prominent examples include white matter fibre tracts in the mammalian brain and arrangements of elongated cells, such as cardiomyocytes in the heart wall. It has been posited that such organisations foliate into locally smooth surfaces to optimise function. However, the recovery of these foliations from a single vector field aligned with the local orientation of the underlying sheets remains an open problem. We address this challenge by introducing a mathematical model of a sheet and developing an algorithm for sheet inference, from measurements of the oriented structures. Given an input vector field, our model estimates a second vector field that is orthonormal to it, while also requiring the Lie bracket of the two to vanish. To balance sheet likelihood against low surface area, we also reduce the mean curvature of the recovered local surface. We compute the first variation of an associated energy and provide a numerical method which admits an efficient, parallel implementation for sheet estimation. We demonstrate our approach on both synthetic and biological examples, motivated by applications to medical imaging. These include white matter fibre tracts from a brain atlas and confocal microscopy images of cleared heart wall tissue. For the latter we are able to reconstruct sheets aligned with local cardiomyocyte directions at unprecedented (micrometre) scale.

title: Authenticating IoT Data on Ethereum after Pectra and Fusaka: A Cost Study of Signature Schemes, Batching and Anchoring for Agricultural Supply Chain Finance
summary: Blockchain-based supply chain finance can turn the sensor-recorded production history of smallholder farms into verifiable credit evidence, but only if every record is authenticated and anchored at a cost that scales to large device fleets. Ethereum's 2025 Pectra and Fusaka upgrades changed this cost landscape: they added precompiles for BLS12-381 and P-256, repriced calldata and MODEXP, and capped transaction gas at $2^{24}$. We organize the authentication and anchoring of IoT records into three trust levels, from posting a Merkle root through a trusted aggregator to verifying every device signature on-chain, and implement four replay-protected signature designs: ECDSA over secp256k1 and P-256, BLS aggregate signatures with on-chain hash-to-curve, and a pseudonymous identity-based signature with batch verification. Measured as signed transactions under the rules before and after both upgrades, the upgrades mainly changed which designs are feasible, not their cost. Batching and Merkle anchoring cut the cost of ECDSA authentication sixfold, to 8,963 gas per record, and secp256k1 ECDSA remains the cheapest authenticated design: P-256 costs 1.6 times as much, the identity-based design 2.7 times and BLS aggregation 3.9 times, dominated by on-chain hashing to the curve. One transaction carries at most 1,754 ECDSA-authenticated records but only 411 BLS-aggregated ones. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, pairing-based signing takes 5.7 ms against 0.29 ms for ECDSA. Pairing-based designs pay off only when the application needs their additional properties, and the identity-based design adds key escrow at the key generation centre. The benchmark harness is released for reproducibility.

title: Hierarchical coupling in tripartite van der Waals cavity magnonics for a low-loss and tunable coupled-mode Hamiltonian
summary: One of the greatest merits of cavity magnonics (CM) is the ability to explore rich coupled-mode physics, driven by the large \textit{in situ} flux tunability of magnonic resonances and magnon--photon coupling. Meanwhile, van der Waals (vdW) magnets offer an ultra-compact and highly integrated implementation of CM without complex fabrication processes. Nonetheless, the substantial magnon losses significantly hinder the combination of all these advantages. Here, we realize a hierarchical anti-crossing structure in a tripartite vdW CM with CrCl3 and realize an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian. We achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in loss while maintaining a strong coupling condition. Additionally, we theoretically confirm the feasibility of simultaneous and \textit{in situ} tuning of both loss and coupling by varying the magnetic field direction and strength. Featuring a micrometer-scale thickness and a width of a few millimeters, our device is significantly smaller than those based on bulk crystals or crystal arrays. Our results establish vdW cavity magnonics as versatile platform for investigating intriguing phenomena predicted in coupled-mode systems.

title: GramStatTexNet: Efficient, Interpretable, and Neuro-Inspired Texture Analysis-by-Synthesis
summary: Deep networks achieve high realism in texture synthesis but often rely on opaque, over-parameterized representations that have limited direct connection to biological vision. Neuroscience-informed pyramid models are interpretable, compact, and biologically inspired, but rely on small, hand-curated statistics sets that are difficult to generalize or extend. We introduce GramStatTexNet, a hybrid analysis-by-synthesis framework that combines the multi-scale Gabor filter structure of classical models with the flexibility of Gramian-based correlations, organized into structured filter families. This structured representation enables analyses that are challenging for deep-feature methods: each statistic carries a named filter-family identity, allowing us to decompose synthesis fidelity into per-family contributions and to learn an interpretable, low-dimensional embedding that preserves perceptual texture content. We compare our framework to classical and deep texture-synthesis baselines across diverse texture categories, and on multiple perceptual metrics, highlighting the compactness and interpretability advantages of this hybrid representation, alongside competitive synthesis quality. This same framework extends naturally to peripheral textures via spatial pooling, and to dynamic textures using a spatiotemporal filter bank. GramStatTexNet provides a unified, interpretable framework for analyzing and modeling visual information with natural extensions across space, time, and eccentricity. Project page: https://vdutell.github.io/gstn

title: ACUS: An Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score for Incomplete-View CT
summary: Sparse-view and limited-arc computed tomography (CT) are commonly treated as projection completion: a network fills an unmeasured view, and the result is ranked by similarity to one ground-truth image. That score can be high even when the query angle is far from every acquired measurement, because a learned prior may invent anatomy the scan never constrained. Existing protocols therefore leave a basic question unanswered: how does predictive reliability change with distance from the acquired views? We propose the Angular Calibrated Uncertainty Score (ACUS) to answer that question. ACUS is the Winkler interval score of a nominal 90% predictive interval on held-out projections, binned by distance to the nearest acquired view. It charges interval width and adds a large miss penalty when a held-out pixel falls outside the interval, so a narrow band helps only when coverage holds. We use collapse on acquired angles as a necessary consistency check on the predictor. On chest and dental cone-beam orbits, interval width grows with the angular gap. Empirical coverage ranges from 77% to 92%, and the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of the point estimate falls as the width rises. Nearest-neighbor, interpolation, and point completion, each given one residual scale, have zero reported far coverage and incur outside-distance penalties. ACUS exposes gap-dependent overconfidence that a point-estimate PSNR alone does not measure.

title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
summary: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

title: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
summary: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it. T/E/S combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Across reasoning and information-seeking tasks, events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for Qwen with LoRA. Span duration and preceding events are associated with transitions, and retaining event history across span boundaries improves prediction. We formulate budget-allocation counting and action-conditional continuation queries, prove counting hardness under explicit encodings, and derive conditions for affordable decision certification. In finite-process experiments, bounds that cancel shared continuation mass recover the same optimal actions as full dynamic programming while reducing mean inference CPU time by 77.7%. On 71 held-out HotpotQA and MuSiQue questions, a compact structural observer improves prediction of whether a fixed inference procedure finishes within a CPU allowance: Brier loss falls from 0.0836 to 0.0756. An annotation audit identifies substantial errors in that observer, separating this computational result from semantic validation of its features.

title: A Comparison of Heuristic, Human-Sensitive, and Self-Play DRL Policies in Human-Agent Teaming
summary: Dynamical Perceptual-Motor Primitives (DPMPs) offer a tractable framework for generating human-like movement dynamics in artificial agents (AAs) and have been used to support coordination in human-AI teaming tasks. Traditionally, DPMP controllers rely on heuristic (rule-based) decision policies derived from human behavior to guide goal selection and action sequencing. Although effective in structured tasks, such heuristics can be difficult to generalize to more complex settings, motivating interest in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for learning decision policies for human-AI interaction. A key challenge, however, is ensuring that DRL policies remain aligned with human strategies, particularly when agents are trained through self-play. To examine this issue, we compared three target-selection policies governing DPMP-based AAs in a first-person herding task: (1) a human-derived heuristic policy, (2) a self-play DRL policy (SP-DRL), and (3) a human-sensitive DRL policy (HS-DRL) trained alongside a heuristic agent. Results showed that heuristic agents most closely matched typical human-human coordination patterns, followed by HS-DRL agents, whereas SP-DRL agents deviated most. These findings highlight the importance of human-informed training when developing DRL-based teammates and suggest that simple heuristic policies may remain an effective approach for designing human-aligned AAs capable of human-AI collaboration.

title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
summary: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.

title: Toward Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Neural AC Power Flow
summary: Growing uncertainty in power system operations from renewables integration, extreme weather, and data center loads challenges the reliability of traditional power flow solvers at scale. Machine learning-based proxies are a potentially promising alternative, but the prohibitive cost of generating training data for large grids makes out-of-distribution generalization a key capability for deployment; currently, models trained on small grids lack that capability. In this work, we systematically evaluate how physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation improve the zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network-based power flow models from smaller systems to a larger, unseen 500-bus system. We find that (1) physics-informed losses improve transfer relative to purely supervised objectives; (2) multi-grid training on smaller systems matches the best single grid but does not close the gap to target-grid training; (3) perturbation-based augmentation on edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%; and (4) random line/generator dropout does not consistently improve performance.

title: AdaS-ViT: Test-Time Adaptive Routing for Spiking Vision Transformers with Ultra-High Energy Efficiency
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise event-driven and energy-efficient vision, yet existing spiking vision transformers (S-ViTs) largely confine spiking tokens to fixed and uniform firing schemes along the temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, whereas suppressing the computational redundancy thus incurred calls for adaptive firing mechanisms that operate jointly across all three axes at test time. To this end, we propose the Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (AdaE-IF) model, which consults the attention score of each spiking token and routes salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns while assigning energy-frugal coarse patterns to the remaining regions. Building on AdaE-IF, we further introduce Spiking Gated Self-Attention (S-GSA) and Spiking Local-Gated Unit (S-LGU), which enforce selective spike emission at token and channel granularity. We integrate the aforementioned mechanisms and modules into AdaS-ViT, a test-time adaptive-routing architecture trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum that stabilizes the co-adaptation of firing precision and routing masks. Extensive experiments across benchmarks spanning diverse data scales and modalities demonstrate that AdaS-ViT consistently achieves highly competitive performance. Notably, on ImageNet-1k it consumes only 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image and attains an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32$\times$ to 72$\times$, operating in an economical inference regime and thereby pushing the energy-efficiency boundary further.

title: When Price Charts Rhyme: Historical Visual Retrieval for Stock Return Prediction
summary: We study whether visually similar price histories predict similar future returns, using a vision model to retrieve each stock's most similar charts from three decades of U.S. price histories. A representation pretrained only on natural images already retrieves neighbors whose realized returns predict the cross-section of stock returns. Aligning the representation with subsequent returns more than doubles the strategy's Sharpe ratio and outperforms a convolutional neural network trained directly on chart images. The predictability is concentrated among stocks with greater limits to arbitrage. Returns and order imbalances around portfolio formation indicate that the signal identifies temporary selling pressure that partially reverts. A sparse autoencoder traces the return-aligned signal to recurring visual states that determine which historical charts are retrieved. Our approach traces each forecast to dated historical charts, making it more transparent than direct image-to-return models and linking rule-based technical analysis with machine-learning chart reading.

title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
summary: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.

title: HypoLoop: Revising Weight-Editing Plans from Scientific Feedback
summary: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction. We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: https://github.com/limengran98/HypoLoop.

title: CoScan: Multi-Scale Content-Adaptive Space-Filling Scans for Causal State-Space Image Restoration
summary: Selective state-space models (SSMs) have recently shown strong potential for efficient image restoration. A central difficulty, however, is that a 2D feature map typically needs to be linearized into a 1D token sequence for causal state-space updates, making restoration performance highly sensitive to the imposed scan order. Existing deterministic scans follow space-filling principles but remain fixed and content-agnostic, and can yield fragmented or semantically inconsistent contexts under degradations. We propose \textbf{CoScan}, a \textbf{co}ntent-adaptive \textbf{scan}-order design for causal vision SSMs. CoScan learns image-dependent space-filling traversals via differentiable proxy supervision driven by \textbf{scan-quality objectives} that \textit{encourage short-range coherence and causal predictability, while preserving spatial adjacency}. To support hierarchical restoration backbones, we introduce an \textbf{efficient multi-scale scan construction by coarsening a fine-level minimum spanning tree}, producing coherent scans across feature resolutions. In addition, a \textbf{frequency-guided start selection strategy} is designed to \textit{place informative structures early in the sequence prefix to strengthen causal context formation}. Plugged into existing Mamba-based backbones, CoScan yields consistent improvements across several restoration benchmarks with minimal overhead and shows promising results on high-level vision tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/dongw22/CoScan

title: ExecGap: Exploiting Command-Execution Gap for Patch Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation. Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities. Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation. This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion. Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks. Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.

title: Producing $μ$Bq/m3-level low-226Ra ultrapure water for the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory
summary: The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), a 20 kton low-background liquid-scintillator (LS) detector, was designed primarily to determine the neutrino mass ordering. JUNO requires ultrapure water (UPW) with a Ra concentration < 50~$μ$Bq/m3 because of the direct liquid-liquid contact between LS and UPW during detector filling. To meet this stringent requirement, a high-sensitivity measurement system capable of detecting Ra in water down to 3.9 $μ$Bq/m3 was developed, and the 100 t/h UPW production process was optimized. By integrating selective ion-exchange resin with membrane-based separation technologies, the system consistently produced UPW with a Ra concentration of <4$μ$Bq/m3, exceeding the JUNO specification and, to our knowledge, representing one of the lowest reported levels achieved at this engineering scale. This paper describes the design and implementation of JUNO's UPW system and the high-sensitivity Ra measurement platform, together with a systematic evaluation of Ra removal efficiencies across the purification train and validation of the final water quality.

title: Helicity-squared scaling of post-eikonal phases for electromagnetic and gravitational waves in Ricci-flat spacetimes
summary: Spin-optical descriptions of electromagnetic and gravitational waves isolate finite-frequency corrections that are odd in the helicity. We study the complementary, helicity-even part of the first post-eikonal correction for scalar, electromagnetic, and linearized gravitational waves on Ricci-flat backgrounds. In a parallel-propagated null tetrad, the direct Weyl coupling of the gravitational field projects onto the circular transverse-traceless states as the multiple $2C_{\bar m m\bar m m}$ of the identity. The Ricci identity for the spin coefficient $μ$ then rewrites this projection as a total derivative plus optical terms. The helicity-even phase of a spin-$s$ wave, measured relative to the scalar wave, then obeys a helicity-squared law, $Δ_2=4Δ_1$, up to endpoint terms. The Weyl coupling is what completes the $h^2$ scaling in the gravitational case. For weak-deflection scattering by a Schwarzschild black hole we evaluate the relevant integrals along the ray and obtain $Δ_s=-3πs^2/(8Mωρ^3)$, with $ρ=b/M$. The same coefficient follows independently, and without reference to any frame or gauge, from the Regge--Wheeler phase shifts combined with the asymptotics of the rotation functions $d^l_{ss}$. Direct numerical integration of the radial equations confirms it. At first order in $M$ the helicity-even phase difference vanishes, as required by the Born amplitudes. The helicity-odd spin-optical sector and the helicity-even post-eikonal sector are therefore organized by the first and second powers of the helicity, respectively.

title: A Hardware-Aware Comprehensive Study of Edge Vision Deployment with A Unified Hardware-Model-Runtime Mapping Framework
summary: The rapid growth of deep learning has driven the deployment of computer vision directly on resource-constrained edge devices. However, the extreme heterogeneity of edge hardware architectures poses major challenges in selecting and designing suitable vision models. This survey bridges the gap between edge hardware constraints, model architectures, and deployment software toolchains. We establish a comprehensive taxonomy classifying edge hardware into three distinct tiers: mid-range devices (GPUs and dedicated NPUs or TPUs), dedicated embedded MPU or SoC processors, and microcontrollers (MCUs). We aggregate and analyze multi-source benchmark results for image classification and object detection across the computing spectrum, spanning from tens of watts down to milliwatt-scale bare-metal MCUs. Based on these empirical findings, we propose a two-tiered hardware-to-model mapping framework that provides concrete model selection matrices across performance priorities (Speed, Balanced, Accuracy) and actionable architectural design principles (peak SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm-compiler co-design). Finally, we highlight critical deployment challenges including toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility, and outline promising future research directions in on-device adaptation and sustainable Edge AI.

title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
summary: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.

title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
summary: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

title: Fast closed-loop STEM navigation using vision-language models with typed decisions
summary: Closed-loop scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), in which each acquired image determines the next field of view and magnification, offers a route to autonomous atomic-scale materials analysis. Such a loop would automate navigation to defects and grain boundaries, a task that has long relied on operator judgment, and would enable systematic analysis of diverse local structures at scale. Realizing it hinges on the decision step, which must translate each acquired image into the next operation both quickly and correctly; yet which decision method can deliver both remains unclear. Here, we isolate this decision step. Using simulated atomic-resolution STEM images of a substitutional W dopant and a grain boundary in monolayer MoS$_2$, where the true target position is known and every method starts from identical conditions, we compared four vision-language models (VLMs) and three decision methods. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of Typed Decision, which directly obtains the probabilities of candidate labels from a pretrained VLM, for closed-loop STEM navigation. Typed Decision showed the shortest decision latency for all models (0.13-0.21 s) and generally achieved the highest navigation success rate among the three methods: it was the best for all models in W dopant navigation (66-91%) and for the best-performing model, Cosmos-Reason2 32B, in grain boundary navigation (43%). Furthermore, navigation to the different targets, the W dopant and the grain boundary, was possible by natural-language specification alone, without task-specific training of the VLM. These results indicate that Typed Decision is an effective decision method for realizing fast, accurate, and flexible closed-loop STEM.

title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
summary: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sco-edge/MoMoVL.

title: MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management
summary:
Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control).
  Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.

title: JEV vs. LLMs: A Comparative Analysis for Phishing Email Detection
summary: Phishing remains a major source of credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email security systems must classify large message volumes reliably, quickly, and at manageable cost. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer flexible text understanding, but their token-based generation increases response time and API cost, and the reliability of their confidence values requires measurement. Jev 1.13, a typed decision model from TypeSafe AI, instead returns a structured outcome with a confidence value. This paper compares Jev 1.13 with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, covering classification performance, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, and probability calibration. Jev achieves the highest accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), and F1 score (82.62%). It also records the shortest batch time (173.88 seconds), the lowest token count (597,895), the lowest cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and the lowest Brier score (0.1698) and ECE (0.1594). These results suggest that Jev is a promising option for fast, structured, high-volume triage. LLMs retain the advantage of generating explanations, which we do not evaluate, and all four systems require further validation before standalone deployment.

title: Axion: A differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework,demonstrated on phase-field fracture
summary: We introduce Axion (Autodifferentiable, XLA-compiled, Implicit, On-device Numerics), a differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework written in JAX. The element kernels, Newton and Krylov iterations, bound-constrained updates, staggered coupling of fields, and the loop over load increments are expressed as a single program that is just-in-time compiled and executed on the GPU without host intervention. Consistent tangent operators are obtained by forward-mode automatic differentiation of the element residual, and derivatives of the discrete solution with respect to model parameters are obtained by differentiating the same program. Global operators are applied element by element without assembling a sparse matrix, octree mesh refinement is performed within fixed-size arrays, and a cell-based domain decomposition runs the same program on several GPUs. Phase-field fracture is implemented as the first module because it combines fine mesh resolution, bound-constrained damage, and repeated nonlinear solves over a loading history, which together make it computationally expensive. On two- and three-dimensional single-edge-notched tension benchmarks, a uniformly refined Axion computation completes faster than the corresponding adaptive FEniCSx computation. At identical discretization, the two-dimensional benchmark runs 37.9 times faster on one GPU than a FEniCSx implementation on one CPU. Strong and weak scaling efficiencies on four GPUs are 92% and 96%, respectively. Large-scale demonstrations include hydraulic fracture in a poroelastic medium (0.38M degrees of freedom), fracture of a multi-material premolar under contact loading (0.69M degrees of freedom), and a concrete gravity dam (96M degrees of freedom) on a single GPU. The implementation is available as open-source software.

title: Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
summary: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
summary: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
summary: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $π_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

title: Learning What to Degrade: A Recoverability-Aware Curriculum for Reliable Smart-Glasses Super-Resolution
summary: Degradations in smart-glasses images obscure small text and fine-grained structures needed by vision-language models (VLMs) for visual assistance. We introduce an high-resolution (HR)-referenced semantic evaluation protocol that compares VLM outputs on restored images with those on corresponding HR references. Our evaluation reveals two failure modes: generative SR can synthesize misleading details, whereas restoration-oriented SR can leave critical evidence blurred or ambiguous. These findings motivate improving faithful detail recovery in restoration-oriented SR, where a key training challenge is to provide sufficiently difficult inputs while retaining recoverable visual information. We propose ReDiC (Recoverability-Difficulty Curriculum), which combines a model-independent recoverability proxy with model-relative restoration difficulty to adapt training degradation severity. ReDiC increases severity when inputs are recoverable and restoration is easy, maintains challenging but recoverable conditions, and reduces severity when estimated recoverability is low. It modifies only training degradation generation, leaving the SR architecture and reconstruction objective unchanged. Across NAFNet, SwinIR, and MambaIR, ReDiC improves average PSNR by approximately 2.5 dB and HR-referenced semantic scores by about 3 points over the corresponding baselines on synthetic benchmarks, with further gains confirmed by LLM-based and human evaluations on 200 real smart-glasses captures.

title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

title: Image-Condition-Controlled Diffusion Network with Large-Scale CT Pretraining for CT-Free Attenuation Correction in Dynamic Cardiac PET
summary: Positron emission tomography (PET) provides quantitative information on myocardial perfusion. In dynamic PET, tracer kinetics are tracked through a series of reconstructed time frames. Reliable attenuation correction is essential for accurate measurements. Clinical attenuation maps ($μ$-maps) are typically derived from computed tomography (CT), which adds radiation exposure and may introduce PET-CT misregistration due to respiratory and cardiac motion. Moreover, supervised CT-free methods rely on paired non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET and CT data, which are scarce, whereas large-scale unpaired CT data are more readily available. To address these challenges, we propose Large-scale Unpaired CT-Informed Diffusion (LUCID), a framework that transfers anatomical priors learned from 10,000 chest CT volumes in the public CT-RATE dataset to $μ$-map synthesis for dynamic cardiac $^{82}$Rb PET. First, a convolutional neural network (CNN) predicts an initial $μ$-map from each NAC PET frame. Second, the CT-pretrained diffusion backbone refines a low-noise perturbation of the CNN prediction through a single denoising step, conditioned on the corresponding NAC PET frame via ControlNet. Finally, frame-wise predictions are averaged voxel-wise to obtain the final $μ$-map. We further introduce the voxel-wise temporal standard deviation (TSD) to quantify inter-frame variability without requiring a reference $μ$-map. We evaluated LUCID on an in-house dataset of 102 patients and found that it achieved the best quantitative accuracy while maintaining competitive inter-frame consistency.
